title: Pairs Whose Sum Lands in a Band
statement:
You get an integer array nums and two integers lower and upper. Count the index pairs (i, j) with i < j where

lower ≤ nums[i] + nums[j] ≤ upper.

Pairs are counted by position, so equal values at different indexes form separate pairs.

examples.why: 4 + 2 = 6, 4 + 3 = 7, -1 + 6 = 5 and 2 + 3 = 5. Every other pair sums below 5 or above 7.
Three different index pairs, all with sum 6. Counting distinct value pairs would give 1.

hints: Pairs are unordered, so the order of nums does not matter for the count. What does sorting buy you?
Count pairs with sum ≤ upper, then subtract the pairs with sum ≤ lower − 1. Each of those is a simpler question.
On a sorted array, count pairs with sum ≤ t using two pointers: if nums[l] + nums[r] ≤ t, every index between l and r pairs with l.

explain.intuition:
The count of pairs only depends on which values exist, not where they sit, so you may sort. A band condition lower ≤ sum ≤ upper is awkward, but "sum ≤ t" is easy, and the band count is atMost(upper) − atMost(lower − 1). It is the same subtraction trick as counting a range with prefix sums.

For atMost(t) on a sorted array, put l at the start and r at the end. If nums[l] + nums[r] ≤ t, then nums[l] plus anything between l and r is also ≤ t, so r − l pairs are counted at once and l moves right. Otherwise nums[r] is too big for every remaining partner and r moves left.
steps: Define atMost(t): l = 0, r = n − 1, count = 0; while l < r, if nums[l] + nums[r] ≤ t add r − l and do l++, else r--.
pitfalls: Forgetting that the result can exceed 2³¹ − 1 for 100 000 elements. Use a 64-bit counter in typed languages.
Subtracting atMost(lower) instead of atMost(lower − 1), which drops pairs whose sum is exactly lower.
Counting a pair twice, or pairing an element with itself, when using binary search over the whole array instead of only the part after i.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Two nested loops over i < j.

solutions.title: Sort and binary search the partner range
solutions.idea: For each i, the valid partners after i form one contiguous range of the sorted array. Find its ends with two binary searches.

solutions.title: Sort and two pointers, twice
solutions.idea: Count pairs with sum at most upper, minus pairs with sum at most lower − 1.

followups: Count pairs whose difference, not sum, lands in the band. What changes?
Numbers arrive one at a time and you must report the running count. Which data structure replaces the sort?
